content: Hi I have been using a fork of Lean4 repo with a built in Lean code formatter for a week. Seems to work relatively reliable. It uses the pretty term formatter of Lean for code and some simple conventions for top level items https://github.com/wvhulle/lean4
Let me know if anyone is interested in up streaming parts of this. :)

While it is not upstreamed, could it live in an external server plugin? This way, it could be run on top of normal lean versions. I wrote a small external LSP plugin once and it was reasonably simple (but I don't know about this case), it was possible to add additional LSP methods with builtin_initalize and registerLspRequestHandler.

Lua Viana Reis said:

While it is not upstreamed, could it live in an external server plugin? This way, it could be run on top of normal lean versions. I wrote a small external LSP plugin once and it was reasonably simple (but I don't know about this case), it was possible to add additional LSP methods with builtin_initalize and registerLspRequestHandler.

I don’t think formatting is possible in user space. The lean4 repo only exposes certain lsp capabilities
It can give it another try to make a seperate extension but the lsp capabilities are kind of hard wired in the server module in lean4 repository

Willem vanhulle said:

Hi I have been using a fork of Lean4 repo with a built in Lean code formatter for a week. Seems to work relatively reliable. It uses the pretty term formatter of Lean for code and some simple conventions for top level items https://github.com/wvhulle/lean4

Cool! I've been planning on writing a Lean formatter for a while, but looks like you beat me to it. :smile:

I tried it out on some of my Lean files and it seems to work great. Also, is there some way to run the formatter as a command-line tool rather than using the "Format Document" option is VSCode?
Are you both aware that the Lean FRO is very actively working on writing a Lean code formatter?
I have seen that message several times over the past years on the Lean FRO blog post and yearly goals, but have not been able to find it. Could I offer any help?
Are you sure you’ve seen that? The roadmaps are all about stuff they would like to do, not about stuff they are very actively working on.

Ah maybe it was on the roadmap that I saw it a while ago. Apologies.

But it seems like everything is ready. The pretty formatter is there. Just need to add the capability to the lsp server and format the things not covered by the pretty formatted like comments. I’ve done that at my fork.

Anything we can do to avoid double work? On which branch is the rest working?

@Willem vanhulle I think I found a bug in your formatter when formatting multiline strings, for instance:

#eval "Hello
world"

gets formatted into 

#eval
  "Hello
    world"

which is already wrong, but if you keep formatting the file, it adds four more spaces each time before world.
Also, is it intentional that the formatter adds an extra newline after comments?

Anthony Wang said:

Willem vanhulle I think I found a bug in your formatter when formatting multiline strings, for instance:

#eval "Hello
world"

gets formatted into 

#eval
  "Hello
    world"

which is already wrong, but if you keep formatting the file, it adds four more spaces each time before world.

Will fix that
It is a problem with the exiting formatter of strings in main (outside of the code i added).
@Anthony Wang Fixed it by removing the problematic behaviour where Lean formatter would add an indent tab to multiline strings
What is the current development status of the formatter being developed by Lean FRO?
Still making progress but not released yet.

Patrick Massot said:

Still making progress but not released yet.

Where can we try it out?
Nowhere yet. It won’t be a secret release, you’ll know when it comes out, don’t worry.

On which branch are you developing?

Patrick Massot said:

Nowhere yet. It won’t be a secret release, you’ll know when it comes out, don’t worry.
It’s okay for things to be unfinished. That’s life. But Lean is also an open source project.
Open source does not imply being developed in the open. It's completely normal for large Lean features to be developed in private and then published when they're ready.
It is sad to see that Lean has become primarily closed development and a closed community for the select few.
That's how Lean core has always operated though.

Personally I feel that as long as core takes feedback and insight from the community, I don’t feel owed a view of the false starts and nitty-gritty problem-solving that go into developing the first version of a complex feature…figuring out the very first version of something in private seems normal to me, even beyond lean per se.

I feel it's worth mentioning that while they can choose to operate as such if they see fit (no one promised open-ness), and some people can be okay with it (and even encourage it), it does go against the spirit of open-source, and IMO is not normal in open-source communities.
There are also other terms for such scenarios, such as "open source, not open contribution" or "source available".
(no shade intended, just felt the need to balance this thread)

Is simply developing v1 of something in private an example of those things, though? It's not like external PRs are rejected out of hand, nor is it the case (I'm guessing) that further iteration won't happen afterwards...but maybe I'm just not familiar enough with open source norms.

This is getting off-topic, but I will point to https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md
There's nothing new there, this is the model that Lean core has used for ages.

If you want to call it "source available", I guess that's fine. [I agree with Chris's clarification below.]

I don't find "source available" an accurate description at all. The distinction in that label is being able to view source code but not necessarily having the right to modify or redistribute. This is simply not the case under an Apache 2.0 license. "Open source, not open contributions" is closer, though still not fully the situation given that there is a procedure for external contributors. And these are both very different from requiring that any in-progress development must occur in a publicly visible branch, which seems unreasonable to me.

Yeah, for loose comparison, there's Lua, which is fully Open Source MIT licensed, and essentially does not accept contributions at all:

Lua is best described as a closed-development, open-source project.
This means that, even though the source code is freely available for scrutiny and adaption, Lua is not developed in a collaborative way.
We do accept user suggestions, but never their code verbatim.
We always try to do our own implementation.

(from https://lua.org/doc/hopl.pdf)

Willem vanhulle said:

On which branch are you developing?

Patrick Massot said:

Nowhere yet. It won’t be a secret release, you’ll know when it comes out, don’t worry.

I think there is some misunderstanding here. I personally have nothing to do with this work. I’m only repeating publicly available information and common sense. And no, open source software never meant you get access to the computer of every contributor to spy in real time on what they are doing. This is the work of a single contributor who has every right to choose when he releases a pre-version. It’s an extraordinarily complicated project that was never attempted before (no other programming language has Lean’s syntax extensibility), and I think he is very wise to take it seriously.

Willem vanhulle said:

It’s okay for things to be unfinished. That’s life. But Lean is also an open source project.

And I don’t think that being condescending and paternalistic will help you to satisfy your curiosity more quickly.

Patrick Massot said:

This is the work of a single contributor who has every right to choose when he releases a pre-version.

Is the formatter not a Lean FRO project?
It is
